newsitem.title: IRAN: Foreign aid trickles to Iran, more expected - U.N.
newsitem.headline: Foreign aid trickles to Iran, more expected - U.N.

text.p: International aid for earthquake victims has started to trickle in after Iran's first appeal for foreign help in at least 10 years, a U.N. official said on Wednesday.
Michael Schulenburg, U.N. resident coordinator in Tehran, said Norway had pledged $135,000, Denmark $30,000 and U.N. agencies in Iran an initial package worth $450,000.
Iran has said Switzerland, Britain, Japan and some international organisations had offered aid. Saudi Arabia said it was sending two plane loads of relief supplies.
"It is not much, but we are optimistic more pledges will be made," Schulenburg told Reuters.

Nearly 1,000 people were killed, 2,600 injured and 36,000 made homeless by Friday's earthquake which measured 5.5 on the Richter scale in a mountainous region in northwest Iran. It was followed by 500 aftershocks and another quake measuring 5.2 on Sunday night.
Rescue teams battled knee-deep snow, freezing temperatures and marauding wolves to search for victims. Schulenburg said he believed the search for survivors had ended.
The U.N. office in Tehran said on Tuesday some 60,000 people were affected by the quake, which completely destroyed 20 villages and damaged 80 others in the agricultural province.
Schulenburg said it was the first time in at least 10 years the Iranian government had issued an official plea for foreign aid.

"On previous occasions they only said they would welcome international aid. This time they issued a formal appeal," he said. "They have a very sophisticated relief system but they are overstretched with having to deal with the Iraqi Kurdish refugees last year, last month's earthquake and now this."

Tens of thousands of Iraqi Kurdish refugees fled fighting in northern Iraq last September, although most have since gone home. Iran hosts around two million refugees from Afghanistan and Iraq, U.N. officials in Tehran said.
In February, two earthquakes measuring 6.1 and 5.4 on the Richter scale killed at least 79 people and injured 260 in northeastern Iran.

Schulenburg said Iran had been quick to put together a list of what was needed. The list included food, clothing, tents, heaters, medicine, the reconstruction of clinics, water and power networks, agricultural equipment, seeds and ambulances.
Diplomats said after an earthquake killed 35,000 people in 1990, international aid poured in but the government did not actually appeal for help.
